design_detail: Naturalistic prospective field study with repeated measures over one week, no placebo and no random allocation. Three self-selected groups of 15 (ten or more earlier occasions of ecstasy use; one to nine; never) were tested four times: drug-free at home before a Saturday night out, at a London nightclub 2 to 8 hours after tablets they chose to take (8 of 30 at 8 to 16 hours), and 2 and 7 days later. Outcomes: 16 single-item visual analogue mood scales, a 16-word auditory recall task (two lists per session) and a computerized visual search task. Two-way (mood, memory) and three-way (visual search) analyses of variance, then one-way analyses of variance at each session with Duncan tests of each ecstasy group against the comparison group. Tape-recorded interviews are quoted in the Discussion but not described in the Methods.
can_establish: How self-rated moods and test scores changed from a drug-free session to a club night and over the following week in a small, self-selected London sample of people who chose to take ecstasy, compared with people at the same club who did not.
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused any of the changes (no placebo, self-chosen tablets of untested content, alcohol and other drugs on the night, sleep and later drug use not recorded), how large or how common a low mood in the days after is among people who use ecstasy, or anything about lasting memory damage (the ecstasy groups already recalled fewer words before the night, and earlier ability was never measured).

sample.recruitment: Community, snowball sampling: word of the study spread among friends and acquaintances who regularly went to a large nightclub in the Epping Forest area of north-east London; participants were unpaid (Materials and methods › Subjects, p. 262).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Groups defined by self-reported lifetime occasions of MDMA use: ten or more, one to nine, or never (p. 262). The baseline session was held only when people were drug-free by their own account: no MDMA for at least 1 week and no other illicit drug for over 24 hours (Procedures and ethics, p. 262). No other inclusion or exclusion criteria (psychiatric or medical history, medicines, pregnancy) are reported.
sample.demographics: Mean age 21.4 (regular group), 22.8 (novice group) and 21.3 (comparison group) years, range 19 to 30; women/men 8/7, 8/7 and 10/5 (p. 262). Education, employment, IQ, psychiatric history, duration of ecstasy use and lifetime use of other drugs are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not reported: the paper does not say whether all 45 attended all four sessions, and no numbers per session are printed. Eight of the 30 people in the ecstasy groups (four per group) were tested at the club 8 to 16 hours after their tablets instead of the planned 2 to 8 hours (p. 263).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers from the social circle of the experimenters around one club, who were told the study's aims beforehand (p. 263) and knew their own group; groups formed by people's own past and planned drug use. The comparison group were clubbers who mostly drank alcohol that night, not a drug-free group, which the authors name as a limit (p. 266). Not representative of people who use ecstasy in general.

exposure.measurement: Self-report only: lifetime occasions of MDMA use for group membership, and the drugs taken that night, noted by each person on a self-rating questionnaire (p. 262). No urine, blood or saliva tests and no testing of the tablets; abstinence before the baseline session also self-reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study condition, as self-reported: 1.80 tablets on average in the regular group and 1.45 in the novice group on the Saturday night; the comparison group took none (abstract, p. 261; p. 262). No spread, range or test of the difference is printed, and the authors describe it as slightly more. Oral tablets (implied, not stated). Lifetime occasions beyond the group cut-offs, frequency and duration of use are not reported. The paper does not discuss tolerance.
exposure.polysubstance: On the night (p. 262): alcohol by 10 of 15 in the comparison group (5.0 drinks per drinker), 5 in the novice group (2.7) and 6 in the regular group (3.7); cannabis by 3, 1 and 2; cocaine by 2, 2 and 4; amphetamine by 1 person in the novice group. The abstract and Discussion call other-drug use at the club similar across groups, without a test. Lifetime and recent use of other drugs, and any drug use between the club night and the 2- and 7-day sessions, are not reported. Nothing was adjusted for.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Baseline: no MDMA for at least 1 week and no other illicit drug for over 24 hours, self-reported, not verified (p. 262). The 2- and 7-day sessions: abstinence since the club night is not reported.

comparison.controls: 15 people from the same social circle who had never taken MDMA, tested at the same club at equivalent times; 10 of them drank alcohol that night, 3 smoked cannabis and 2 took cocaine (pp. 262-263).
comparison.matching: Not matched by design; ages and sex ratios described as similar (21.3 against 21.4 and 22.8 years; women/men 10/5 against 8/7 and 8/7), not tested (p. 262).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure of earlier cognitive ability, education, IQ, mood or psychiatric history. At the drug-free baseline the ecstasy groups already recalled fewer words (12.0 and 13.9 against 15.1 of 32) and the novice group already rated itself sadder (31 against 22) (Table 2, p. 264). Sleep, food and fluid intake, and hangover were not measured at any session.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Yes: mainly alcohol on the night (10 of 15; 5.0 drinks per drinker), with cannabis (3) and cocaine (2); lifetime use of other drugs not reported (p. 262).

outcomes.instruments: Auditory word recall: lists of 16 words heard over headphones at one word every 2 s, written free recall after 30 s, two lists per session (maximum 32, per the axis of Fig. 1), eight lists rotated across sessions and matched for word frequency and length (p. 262; Fig. 1, p. 265). Visual search on an Apple Newton Messagepad: target letter L among X (easy) or T (hard) distractors in arrays of 2 x 2 to 5 x 5, of which only 2 x 2 and 4 x 4 were analysed; response time in seconds (p. 262; Fig. 2, p. 265). Sixteen unipolar visual analogue mood scales from 0 (do not feel at all) to 100 (feel completely) on the same device: abnormal, calm, clearheaded, depressed, drowsy, energetic, good tempered, ill, interested, quick witted, sad, sober, steady, unpleasant, unsociable and well co-ordinated (p. 262; Table 2, p. 264). Tape-recorded interviews quoted in the Discussion (pp. 265-267), method not described.
outcomes.validity_norms: The recall task is cited as sensitive to scopolamine and the visual search task to alcohol (earlier work by the first author and others, p. 262). No validity data or norms for the single-item mood scales. The mood list has no items on elation or empathy, which the authors note may have made it insensitive to the effects people seek (p. 267).
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment or a mood difference means a lower or higher group mean than the comparison group at a session on a Duncan test, with p < 0.10 reported as a borderline trend; change over the week is read from the group means at each session and the group-by-session interaction (pp. 263-264).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 21 measures (16 mood scales, word recall and four visual-search conditions) at four sessions, each ecstasy group compared with the comparison group by Duncan's multiple range test, a lenient post hoc procedure: 168 comparisons (editors' count), with p < 0.10 reported as trends. Some results at p < 0.05 would be expected by chance alone.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None reported. The experimenter recruited and knew the participants and their groups and tested them, including at the club; the mood ratings are self-ratings by people who knew the study's aims; who scored the written recall, and whether blind to group, is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Not computable: the paper prints group means only (Table 2, p. 264) and significance symbols (Tables 1 and 2), with no SDs, F values, degrees of freedom or intervals; Figs 1 and 2 show standard-error bars, which were not read as numbers. Key means (comparison, novice, regular): mood on 0 to 100 scales, at the club sad 20, 9 and 9 (both p < 0.10), abnormal 36, 64 and 74 (both p < 0.01), good tempered 85, 90 and 88; 2 days later sad 22, 56 and 53 (both p < 0.01), depressed 36, 59 (p < 0.01) and 48 (p < 0.10), unsociable 16, 39 (p < 0.01) and 33 (p < 0.05); 7 days later no difference on these. Word recall of 32: baseline 15.1, 13.9 (p < 0.10) and 12.0 (p < 0.01); club 13.5, 9.6 and 8.1 (both p < 0.01); 2 days 12.9, 11.9 and 11.1 (p < 0.05); 7 days 13.4, 11.7 and 11.4 (both p < 0.05). Visual search, 4 x 4 hard, at the club 4.1, 6.9 (p < 0.10) and 8.9 s (p < 0.01). Editors' calculation: at the club the novice and regular groups recalled 71% and 60% of the comparison group's mean (the paper says 60-70%).
analysis.covariates: None. No adjustment for age, sex, alcohol or other drugs on the night, sleep, the timing of the club session or the baseline differences.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Study published in 1998; no protocol or registration is reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only two of the four visual-search array sizes were analysed, by the authors' stated choice of two levels of difficulty (p. 262). All 16 mood scales are reported in Table 2. The novice and regular groups were never compared with each other, although the Discussion ranks them (p. 266). Interview excerpts are quoted with no method and no account of how they were chosen (pp. 265-267).
analysis.power: No power calculation; 15 people per group.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 45 self-selected people around one London club, the two ecstasy groups did not rate their moods clearly better than other clubbers on the night (only p < 0.10 trends for less sadness, and higher 'abnormal' ratings). Two days later they rated their moods lower than the comparison group: sadness and unsociability in both groups; depression, unpleasantness and lower good temper at p < 0.05 in the novice group but only at p < 0.10 in the regular group. Seven days later the groups were alike again. Word recall was lower in the ecstasy groups at the club and, for the regular group, at every session including the drug-free one before the night. No spread, effect sizes or correction for 168 comparisons is reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says that two days afterwards the people in the ecstasy groups, taken together, felt significantly more depressed, abnormal, unsociable, unpleasant and less good tempered than the comparison group; at p < 0.05 this holds for the novice group, but for the regular group only for abnormal and unsociable (p. 261 against Table 2, p. 264). The abstract also says both tasks were significantly impaired on-MDMA, while at the club the novice group did not reach p < 0.05 on any visual-search condition (Table 2). The abstract and Discussion read the drug-free memory differences as suggesting MDMA neurotoxicity in humans, and the Discussion finds consistent evidence that they may reflect serotonergic neurodegeneration "directly caused by MDMA self-administration" (p. 266), although the groups were self-selected, already differed before the night and earlier ability was not measured; the alternatives (chance, self-selection, other drugs) are set aside mainly by appeal to other studies, and for other drugs by similar use on the one night rather than lifetime use. The low moods are attributed to serotonin depletion, which was not measured (pp. 266-267). In the paper's favour, it reports plainly that the ecstasy groups showed no mood advantage at the club, calls this unexpected and discusses context, expectancy, the comparison group's drinking and ceiling effects (pp. 266-267).

timeline.event: Curran and Travill (Addiction): 12 people who used ecstasy and 12 who drank alcohol, at a Saturday dance and 1 and 4 days later; better moods on the night and worse in the days after by group-by-time interaction, but no drug-free baseline and no analysis of each session separately (as described in this paper, p. 262). Not read for this card; no reference record yet.
This study: the first, by its own account, to test mood and cognition at a club against a drug-free baseline (p. 267).

Parrott's review of chronic tolerance cites this study's tablet figures correctly (1.45 against 1.80, p. 74) but calls the regular group more than 10 occasions (here ten or more) and treats the figures as an index of chronic tolerance, which this paper does not discuss; it also lists this study among those showing an association between past use and neurocognitive impairment (p. 77), although the novice and regular groups were never compared statistically here.

replication.where_it_stands: For mood, the two-day low agrees in direction with the one earlier club study the paper cites (Curran and Travill, 1997), whose session-by-session differences were not analysed; later field studies of the days after were not read for this card. For memory, the comparison is in effect cross-sectional (the differences were present before the night) and belongs with the contested literature on lasting effects, not as evidence of change. The tablet figures are reported correctly in the 2005 review that uses them.

funding.funder: None stated. The acknowledgements (p. 267) thank Dr Brian Tiplady (Astra Pharmaceuticals) for the loan of his Apple Messagepad cognitive test system, and John Turner for comments and suggestions.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors: Department of Psychology, University of East London (p. 261). The first author is the sole author of the 2005 review (card sc_parrott_2005) that cites this study's tablet figures. The study was approved by the University Ethics Committee, with written informed consent (p. 263).

what_would_settle_it: A larger prospective study at real events in which the pills are drug-checked (content and amount measured) and use is checked biologically, with a comparison group at the same events whose alcohol and other drug use is measured, daily mood ratings for a week on scales that include the effects people seek, sleep and later drug use recorded, raters or analysts blind to group where possible, and spread and effect sizes reported.

domains.note: People chose their own drugs and nothing was adjusted for. On the night the comparison group mostly drank alcohol (10 of 15; 5.0 drinks per drinker) and cocaine was taken by 4 of 15 in the regular group against 2 in each other group; sleep, food, fluids, hangover and drug use after the night were not measured. The drug-free baseline and repeated measures handle stable differences between people for mood, but the groups already differed before the night on word recall and, in the novice group, on sadness; for the memory differences alone, confounding would be very high.
Self-reported tablets of untested content and self-reported lifetime occasions; no biological check of use on the night or of abstinence before the baseline.

Unpaid volunteers from the experimenters' social circle around one club, by snowball sampling; taking part and group membership both depend on people's own drug use; the direction of any bias is unclear.
No intervention after the club night is described; drug use after the night is a confounding problem, noted above.
Attendance at each session and any missing values are not reported; 8 of 30 were tested later than planned at the club.

Single-item self-ratings by people who knew the study's aims and their own group, tested by an experimenter who knew them, at a noisy club for the second session; low moods in the days after ecstasy were already a described expectation (the paper cites it, p. 262). Whether recall was scored blind is not stated.

168 uncorrected comparisons with a lenient post hoc test and p < 0.10 reported as trends; two of four visual-search array sizes analysed; significance symbols only, with no test statistics or spread; interviews quoted without a method.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four domains are at high risk and they act together on the results this card is cited for: tablets of untested content and self-reported use, a comparison group that drank alcohol, sleep and later drug use not recorded, self-ratings by participants who knew the aims and their own group, an experimenter who knew them, and 168 uncorrected comparisons reported as significance symbols only. Under ROBINS-E, high risk in several domains that together substantially lower confidence in the result gives very high overall. The design still has what most studies of people who use ecstasy lack: a drug-free session before the night, a comparison group at the same club, and repeated measures over a week. The card may be cited for what this sample reported: tablets noted on the night, as a study condition, and self-rated moods at the club and 2 and 7 days later against other clubbers, with these limits. It may not be cited for what MDMA itself does, for how large or how common a low mood in the days after is, or for memory damage: the ecstasy groups already recalled fewer words before the night, and earlier ability was not measured.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: 45 unpaid volunteers aged 19 to 30, recruited by snowball sampling among friends and acquaintances who regularly went to one large nightclub in north-east London, in three self-selected groups of 15: ten or more earlier occasions of ecstasy use (regular group; mean age 21.4; women/men 8/7), one to nine (novice group; 22.8; 8/7) and never (comparison group; 21.3; 10/5). No placebo and no random allocation; each person was tested four times: drug-free at home before a Saturday night out, at the club, and 2 and 7 days later.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 261); Materials and methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 262); Procedures and ethics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 262-263)

key_findings.finding: Drugs on the night, as each person noted them on a questionnaire: the regular group 1.80 tablets on average and the novice group 1.45 (the authors: slightly more), the comparison group none; no spread, range or test of the difference is printed and the tablets were not tested. Alcohol: 10 of 15 in the comparison group (5.0 drinks per drinker), 5 in the novice group (2.7) and 6 in the regular group (3.7); cannabis 3, 1 and 2; cocaine 2, 2 and 4; amphetamine 1 in the novice group.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 261); Materials and methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 262)
key_findings.note: These are the tablet figures Parrott (2005, p. 74) cites, correctly; the review calls the regular group more than 10 occasions (here ten or more) and uses the figures as an index of chronic tolerance, which this paper does not discuss. Study conditions only.

key_findings.finding: Session timing: the baseline was held when people were drug-free by their own account (no MDMA for at least 1 week, no other illicit drug for over 24 hours), at their own or the experimenter's home, before the planned night out; the club session was held in a quieter area of a noisy, crowded venue, planned for 2 to 8 hours after the tablets (the comparison group at equivalent times), but 8 of the 30 in the ecstasy groups (four per group) were tested 8 to 16 hours after; the 2- and 7-day sessions were at venues similar to the baseline.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Procedures and ethics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Mood at the club (0 to 100 self-ratings, means; comparison, novice, regular; Duncan tests against the comparison group): good tempered 85, 90 and 88 (no difference); sad 20, 9 and 9 (both p < 0.10); depressed 31, 22 and 20 (regular p < 0.10); abnormal 36, 64 and 74 (both p < 0.01); energetic 51, 62 and 64 and interested 68, 80 and 82 (no difference). The comparison group was less sober (46 against 78, p < 0.05, and 67) and less steady (50 against 76, p < 0.05, and 71, p < 0.10), which the authors attribute to alcohol.

Mood 2 days later: sad 22, 56 and 53 (both p < 0.01); unsociable 16, 39 (p < 0.01) and 33 (p < 0.05); abnormal 6, 23 (p < 0.05) and 26 (p < 0.01); depressed 36, 59 (p < 0.01) and 48 (p < 0.10); unpleasant 15, 36 (p < 0.01) and 28 (p < 0.10); good tempered 85, 65 (p < 0.05) and 72 (p < 0.10); energetic 72, 62 and 56 (regular p < 0.05); drowsy 23, 33 and 35 (regular p < 0.10); steady 95, 93 and 90 (regular p < 0.05); calm, ill, interested and quick witted did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, mood-scale rows, columns '2 days after'

key_findings.finding: Mood 7 days later: no difference on sad (22, 25 and 21), depressed (37, 37 and 39), unsociable (22, 18 and 18), unpleasant (14, 18 and 16), abnormal (6, 6 and 5) or good tempered (86, 84 and 87); both ecstasy groups rated themselves less drowsy than the comparison group (28, p < 0.05, and 25, p < 0.01, against 38) and the regular group better co-ordinated (91 against 82, p < 0.10).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, mood-scale rows, columns '7 days after'

key_findings.finding: Before the night (drug-free baseline): the novice group rated itself sadder (31 against 22, p < 0.05) and more depressed (45 against 36, p < 0.10) than the comparison group; both ecstasy groups rated themselves more clearheaded (92 and 94 against 86, p < 0.05), and the regular group less drowsy (27 against 44, p < 0.10).

Two-way analyses of variance (group by session) of the 16 mood scales: interaction p < 0.001 for abnormal, depressed and sad; p < 0.01 for sober, unpleasant and unsociable; p < 0.05 for good tempered and steady; not significant for calm, clearheaded, drowsy, energetic, ill, interested, quick witted and well co-ordinated. Group main effects: abnormal p < 0.001; sad and well co-ordinated p < 0.05; depressed, sober and unpleasant p < 0.10. No F values or degrees of freedom are printed.

Word recall (words recalled of 32; comparison, novice, regular): baseline 15.1, 13.9 (p < 0.10) and 12.0 (p < 0.01); at the club 13.5, 9.6 and 8.1 (both p < 0.01); 2 days later 12.9, 11.9 and 11.1 (p < 0.05); 7 days later 13.4, 11.7 and 11.4 (both p < 0.05). Group and session main effects p < 0.001, interaction p < 0.01. The regular group's lower scores were present before the night, and the novice and regular groups were not compared with each other.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 263); Table 2, row 'Memory word recall' (p. 264); Fig. 1, axis label (p. 265)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: at the club the novice and regular groups recalled 71% and 60% of the comparison group's mean; the paper says 60-70%.

key_findings.finding: Visual search (response time in seconds; comparison, novice, regular): 4 x 4 hard array at the club 4.1, 6.9 (p < 0.10) and 8.9 (p < 0.01), at baseline 2.5, 2.7 and 2.7, at 2 days 3.2, 3.0 and 3.5 and at 7 days 3.6, 3.6 and 3.5. At the club the regular group was slower than the comparison group in all four conditions (one only at p < 0.10) and the novice group reached p < 0.05 in none. At baseline both ecstasy groups were slower on the easy 2 x 2 condition (1.9 and 1.8 against 1.2; p < 0.01 and p < 0.05).
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Assessment measures, 2nd paragraph (p. 262); Table 2, visual search rows (p. 264); Fig. 2 (p. 265)

key_findings.finding: The authors' reading of the moods: the lack of better moods in the ecstasy groups on the night was unexpected; they offer as reasons that most clubbers would expect a good night out (earlier studies mostly had no comparison group of other clubbers), the comparison group's own drinking and drug use, ratings such as good tempered already near the top of the scale, and a mood list without items on elation or empathy. They conclude that the good moods of all the clubbers show the importance of context and expectancy, and describe marked mood swings over the week in the ecstasy groups against fairly stable moods in the comparison group, which they attribute to serotonin depletion (not measured).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs (p. 266, the 7th continued on p. 267) and 9th paragraph (p. 267)

key_findings.finding: Interview excerpts (method not described): people in the ecstasy groups described difficulty with the tasks at the club, mid-week low moods and crying (their own, and among friends who used more drugs), vomiting after each occasion, paranoid feelings, tingling and involuntary arm movements, and two severe emergencies, one about the speaker's partner, who was taken to hospital, and one in which the speaker collapsed at a dance on holiday. These are individual accounts, not measured outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 265, continued on p. 266), 7th paragraph (continued on p. 267) and 8th paragraph (p. 267)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that two days afterwards the people in the ecstasy groups, taken together, felt significantly more depressed, abnormal, unsociable, unpleasant and less good tempered than the comparison group. In Table 2 this holds at p < 0.05 for the novice group; for the regular group only abnormal and unsociable reach p < 0.05, while depressed, unpleasant and good tempered are at p < 0.10. Sad, significant in both groups, is not in the abstract's list.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two-day low is clearer in the novice group than in the regular group; any claim should give the results by group rather than for both ecstasy groups together.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says performance on both tasks was significantly reduced on-MDMA; in Table 2 the novice group does not reach p < 0.05 on any of the four visual-search conditions at the club (one at p < 0.10). The abstract's on-the-night trend for less sadness/depression is p < 0.10 for sadness in both groups but for depression only in the regular group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The visual-search slowing on the night is shown for the regular group only, against a comparison group that had mostly drunk alcohol.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion lists calmness among the moods that fluctuated markedly over the week in the ecstasy groups (p. 267), but Table 1 shows no significant session or interaction effect for calm and Table 2 shows calm between 73 and 86 in every group at every session; Fig. 3, cited for the point, shows neither calm nor depression.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor overstatement of the mood swings; the scales that changed are those in Table 1 with significant interactions.

reporting_issues.issue: The regular group is defined as ten or more earlier occasions in the abstract and Methods (pp. 261-262), but as more than ten occasions in the Discussion (pp. 266, 267); the 2005 review repeats more than 10.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: people with exactly ten occasions belong to the regular group.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Discussion call other-drug use at the club similar across groups (pp. 261, 266), but the counts in the Methods (p. 262) are untested and show cocaine use by 4 of 15 in the regular group against 2 in each other group, and alcohol by 10 of 15 in the comparison group against 5 and 6.
reporting_issues.consequence: Differences in cocaine and alcohol use on the night cannot be excluded as contributors to the differences at the club and two days later.

reporting_issues.issue: Tape-recorded interviews are quoted at length in the Discussion (pp. 265-267), including side effects and two medical emergencies, but the Methods do not mention interviews: who was interviewed, when, how many people and how quotations were chosen are not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The interview material is anecdote, not study data, and cannot support claims about how often anything happens.

reporting_issues.issue: No SDs, F values, degrees of freedom or exact p values are printed anywhere; Tables 1 and 2 give significance symbols only, and the number of people at each session is not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes and their precision cannot be computed, and attrition cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation slips: Squier et al. is cited as 1995 in the text (pp. 261, 266) and listed as 1996 in the references (p. 268); Maxwell et al. is cited as 1994 (p. 261) and 1993 (p. 267) and listed as 1994 (p. 268); Tiplady (1996) in the text is listed as Triplady (p. 268).
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the findings; noted for anyone tracing the cited cases.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 261-268, all pages (PDFs/MDMA/Parrott_1998_SaturdayNightDance.pdf in the senior author's upload folder); Tables 1 and 2 checked on rendered pages; Figs 1 to 3 seen on the rendered page, with values taken from Table 2 rather than read from the figures; no supplementary material exists
